title: Recursion and Backtracking
summary: Factorial, towers of Hanoi, subsets, permutations, N-Queens

guide.title: Solve a big problem with a smaller copy of itself
points: Many problems are naturally self-similar: a folder holds folders, a tree holds subtrees, a list of choices holds smaller lists of choices.
Recursion is the base of backtracking, divide and conquer (merge sort, quick sort), tree and graph search and dynamic programming.
Interviewers use it to see whether you can trust a smaller answer and build on it.

guide.title: Recursion in real software
points: File explorers and "du" walk folders inside folders to compute sizes.
Browsers walk the HTML tree (the DOM) recursively to draw a page; JSON parsers read nested objects the same way.
Compilers evaluate expressions like (2 + 3) × (4 − 1) by recursing on each bracket.
Puzzle solvers (Sudoku, N-Queens) and route planners try a choice, recurse, and undo it: backtracking.

guide.title: Base case + smaller step
points: Base case: the smallest input you can answer directly (n = 0, an empty list, a leaf).
Recursive step: shrink the input, call yourself, and combine the result.
Trust the call: assume solve(n − 1) is right and only think about one level.
Each call waits on the call stack until its child returns; that is how the answer comes back up.

guide.title: Factorial in your language
points: Every recursive function has the same shape: stop, or call yourself on something smaller.

code.python:
def fact(n):
    if n <= 1:                 # base case
        return 1
    return n * fact(n - 1)     # smaller step

guide.title: Backtracking: choose, explore, undo
points: To list all subsets, at each element decide "take it" or "skip it", recurse, then undo the choice.
The same template gives permutations, combinations, N-Queens and word search.
Copy the current path when you save an answer; it keeps changing afterwards.

guide.title: Count the calls
points: Cost = number of calls × work per call. fact(n) makes n calls: O(n).
Two calls per level (subsets, naive Fibonacci) give about 2ⁿ calls: fine for n ≤ 20, hopeless for n = 50.
Memory: the call stack is as deep as the longest chain of calls, O(depth).
Repeated sub-calls with the same arguments? Store the answers (memoisation): that is dynamic programming.

guide.title: What breaks recursive code
points: No base case, or a step that does not shrink the input: infinite recursion and a stack overflow.
Forgetting to return the recursive result (writing solve(n − 1) instead of return solve(n − 1)).
Sharing one list between branches without undoing the change, or saving it without a copy.
Very deep recursion (10⁵ levels) can overflow the stack: Python stops at about 1000 by default. Use a loop or an explicit stack.

guide.title: For advanced learners and interviews
points: Draw the recursion tree for a small input; it shows the cost and the repeated work at a glance.
Prune early in backtracking: stop a branch as soon as it cannot lead to an answer (sum already too big).
Divide and conquer: split into halves, solve each, merge (merge sort, fast power, counting inversions). The master theorem gives the cost.
Next step: Searching and Sorting, where divide and conquer pays off.

problems.statement: Return x raised to n (n >= 0) using recursion in O(log n) steps.
problems.hint: x^n = (x^(n/2))², times x when n is odd.

problems.title: Subsets that reach a sum
problems.statement: Return how many subsets (by position) add up to target. The empty subset sums to 0. At most 20 numbers.
inputFormat: nums: integers separated by spaces (may be empty)
problems.hint: For each element: take it or skip it.

problems.title: All permutations
problems.statement: The string has distinct characters (at most 6). Return all permutations in sorted order, space separated.
problems.hint: Pick each unused character, recurse, then un-pick.

problems.title: Generate parentheses
problems.statement: Return all well-formed strings of n pairs of parentheses, in the order produced by trying "(" before ")".
problems.hint: Add ")" only when there are more "(" than ")".

problems.title: N-Queens count
problems.statement: Return the number of ways to place n queens on an n×n board so that no two attack each other (1 <= n <= 9).
problems.hint: One queen per row; track used columns and both diagonals.
